amstar2_items.justification: Research questions (Section 1, p. 2) and selection criteria (Section 2.2, p. 3) define Population (households in developing countries), Exposure/context (unreliability in performance or functionality of domestic water supply systems), and Outcomes (coping strategies, coping costs, socio-economic distribution, health/social outcomes, effectiveness), but no Comparator group is defined because the included studies are descriptive cross-sectional and qualitative studies.

No a priori review protocol or registration (e.g., PROSPERO) is reported; Section 2.3 cites Hellebrandt et al.'s protocol [26] only as the source from which quality appraisal domains were adapted, with no protocol or deviation reporting for this review itself.

Inclusion criteria specify only 'Based on empirical research' and exclude papers merely listing coping strategies without detail, without explaining or justifying the selection of specific quantitative or qualitative study designs.

Authors searched seven bibliographic databases (CINAHL EBSCOHost, Embase Ovid, PubMed Central, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Scirus, Web of Knowledge), provided the exact Boolean search string, searched grey literature via Google and Google Scholar (first 50 hits), and screened reference lists (identifying 4 studies). However, exact search dates were omitted and the English-only language restriction was noted only as a limitation in Discussion rather than methodologically justified, failing strict AMSTAR 2 criteria for full/partial compliance if language justification is required; rated Partial Yes noting the restriction caveat.

Study selection was not reported as performed in duplicate; Author Contributions (p. 18) state that Batsirai Majuru performed the literature search and drafted the manuscript while co-authors critically reviewed the manuscript.
No duplicate data extraction or independent verification process is described in Methods or Author Contributions.

Figure 1 reports that 13 full-text studies were excluded ('not fully meeting inclusion criteria'), but no bibliography or study-by-study list of excluded full texts with individual exclusion reasons is provided.

Table 2 reports study objectives, setting/location, type of water supply, and sample/design, and Table 3 maps coping strategies across all included studies; however, quantitative outcome/cost estimates and study timeframes are not systematically tabulated, and Cook et al. (2016) [28] was inadvertently omitted from Table 2 despite appearing in Tables 1 and 3.

Quality appraisal (Section 2.3, Table 1) adapted generic reporting items from Hellebrandt et al. [26] (clarity of objective, description of methods/conditions, reporting of results, researcher bias, other validity issues) summed into a 0-12 composite score. It conflates reporting quality with risk of bias and does not systematically evaluate confounding, non-response bias, or measurement validity required for observational cross-sectional studies.

Funding sources for individual included primary studies are not systematically extracted or reported (aside from incidental mention of World Bank sponsorship for early conceptual studies [16, 18, 21]).
No meta-analysis or statistical pooling was performed; the authors used a thematic narrative synthesis due to disciplinary and methodological heterogeneity.

Although Table 1 classifies 3 studies as high risk of bias ([16/17], [29], [44]) and 14 as moderate risk of bias, the Results and Discussion rely heavily on high-risk studies (notably Chaminuka & Nyatsanza 2013 [29]) without qualifying specific synthesis findings or conducting sensitivity discussion by study risk of bias.

Sections 3.3 and 4 explicitly examine heterogeneity in coping cost-to-income ratios and willingness-to-pay estimates across settings, attributing variation to local hydrological/infrastructure context, erosion of consumer trust in utilities, and differences in which cost components (such as travel time valuation) were measured.
Page 18 explicitly states 'Conflicts of Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest' (though specific funding support for conducting the review itself is not stated).

raw_response.methodological_notes: Self-described systematic review with PRISMA-style selection flow diagram (Figure 1), explicit Boolean search string across 7 bibliographic databases plus Google/Google Scholar and backward citation tracking, custom risk-of-bias scoring (Table 1), study characteristics table (Table 2), coping-strategy matrix (Table 3), and thematic narrative synthesis of 28 empirical cross-sectional/qualitative studies (30 publications, as Humplick et al. 1993 [16] + Madanat & Humplick 1993 [17] and Zérah 1998 [23] + Zérah 2000 [24] share datasets and were each counted as 1 study by the authors; all 30 publications are extracted in included_primary_studies to ensure complete overlap detection). Rated borderline_narrow_c2 because the review's primary inclusion criteria and synthesis target behavioural/economic household coping strategies and averting expenditures/willingness-to-pay for infrastructurally unreliable water supplies rather than legal or regulatory rules per se, although property ownership/land tenure (Abstract; Section 3.2), mandatory fixed utility bills/tariffs (Section 3.3), illegal pipe connections (Section 3.1.1), and regulatory oversight of pro-poor/informal water services (Gerlach & Franceys 2009 [39]; Discussion p. 16) appear as secondary sub-themes. Internal reporting discrepancies noted during audit: (1) text cross-references to Table 1 and Table 2 on pp. 4-5 are swapped; (2) text p. 5 reports 12 low, 13 moderate, and 3 high RoB studies, whereas Table 1 lists 11 low, 14 moderate, and 3 high RoB studies; and (3) Cook et al. (2016) [28] is included in Table 1, Table 3, and Results text (rural Kenya) but was inadvertently omitted from Table 2 (leaving 27 rows in Table 2). AMSTAR 2 overall confidence is Critically Low due to multiple critical flaws: no pre-registered protocol (Q2), no list of the 13 excluded full-text articles (Q7), an adapted reporting-heavy quality score that does not adequately assess observational confounding/selection/measurement bias (Q9), and lack of RoB-stratified interpretation despite heavy reliance on high-RoB studies in Results (Q13).
